strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: existing Dynamic Novel View Synthesis (DyNVS) benchmarks primarily focus on photorealism for rigid bodies or simple single-material deformations, lacking multi-body interactions and ground-truth physics information.

Comprehensive coverage of physical phenomena and material types: spans liquids, gases, viscoelastic substances, and textiles, each simulated using well-established domain solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, Vellum in Houdini).

Provides valuable ground-truth physical annotations, including 3D particle trajectories and physical parameters (e.g., Young's modulus, viscosity, temperature), which are crucial for evaluating physics-grounded dynamic modeling.

Extensive benchmarking and clear analysis: evaluates multiple representative 4D/dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM) across both monocular and multi-view setups, clearly demonstrating the failure modes and divergence between RGB photometric fitting and actual physical motion fidelity.
High reproducibility and extensibility: provides simulation node graphs and integration pipelines, enabling users to generate additional modalities (depth, normals) and customize scenes.
weaknesses: The dataset scale is relatively small, consisting of 17 scenes (4–5 scenes per material category). While comparable to early NeRF-style benchmarks, a fully synthetic procedural pipeline could have supported a larger number of procedural variants.

The paper emphasizes the provision of ground-truth physical parameters and 3D particle trajectories for quantitative physics evaluation, but the experimental section evaluates existing methods almost entirely on standard 2D photometric metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), with trajectory analysis limited to qualitative visual comparisons (Figure 6). Incorporating formal 3D trajectory error metrics (e.g., average trajectory error / EPE) or inverse physics parameter estimation benchmarks (such as PAC-NeRF or PhysTwin) would substantially strengthen the benchmark's claims.
The rendering resolution (640 x 720) and camera count (2 to 4 training views) are relatively modest compared to modern 4D benchmarks.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in Dynamic Novel View Synthesis (DyNVS): bridging the gap between perceptual photorealism and underlying physical plausibility.

The dataset covers diverse physical regimes (liquids, gases, viscoelastic substances, and textiles) using appropriate, high-standard numerical solvers in SideFX Houdini (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, and Vellum), incorporating rich multi-body interactions and dynamic contact.

Provides valuable ground-truth physical parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature fields) and 3D particle trajectories that are fundamentally unobtainable from real-world video capture.

Comprehensive benchmark experiments evaluating prominent dynamic Gaussian Splatting baselines (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM) across both monocular and multiview setups, clearly exposing current limitations in capturing complex multi-body physical dynamics.
High reproducibility and extensibility: providing procedural simulation node graphs, COLMAP initializations, and integration pipelines for standard DyNVS frameworks.
weaknesses: The central motivation of the paper is to enable quantitative evaluation of physical modeling and trajectory tracking, yet the experimental evaluation only benchmarks standard photometric image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Trajectory alignment is discussed only qualitatively in Figure 6, without quantitative trajectory error metrics (e.g., mean squared trajectory error, chamfer distance over time) or parameter estimation error.

Absence of physics-informed DyNVS baselines: While the paper evaluates appearance-based DyNVS methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM), it does not benchmark any physics-augmented methods mentioned in the related work (such as PAC-NeRF, Spring-Gaus, or PhysTwin) to demonstrate how physics priors improve trajectory or parameter recovery on this dataset.

Relatively small dataset scale: 17 scenes across four material classes (4 to 5 scenes per category) is somewhat limited for a dedicated benchmark, especially given that some scenes (e.g., single flag, simple smoke) feature very basic dynamics.

Visual realism and rendering environment: Many scenes feature stylized or simplistic visual elements (e.g., flat checkerboard ground planes, basic point lights, simple primitive shapes), which creates a noticeable domain gap compared to real-world visual dynamics.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in dynamic novel view synthesis (DyNVS) by moving beyond visual appearance toward physics-aware multi-body dynamic scene modeling.
Comprehensive coverage of diverse material categories (liquids, gases, viscoelastic substances, and textiles) generated using dedicated, standard physics solvers in Houdini (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, Vellum).
Provides rich ground-truth annotations including simulation parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio) and 3D particle trajectories, along with full simulation graphs and camera setups.

Benchmarking of state-of-the-art dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, SOM) reveals notable performance drops and visual/dynamic failure modes when handling complex multi-body interactions.
weaknesses: Despite emphasizing ground-truth 3D particle trajectories and physics parameters as primary contributions, the experimental evaluation is limited to standard RGB image reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). No quantitative metrics (e.g., 3D tracking error, flow error, or inverse parameter estimation accuracy) are reported to benchmark physical fidelity.
The dataset scale is relatively modest, comprising only 17 scenes in total (4 to 5 scenes per material category), which limits its capacity for training data-driven dynamic priors.

The paper does not propose a baseline or method that effectively leverages the ground-truth physical quantities or integrates multi-physics solvers, leaving the actionable utility of the physics annotations unvalidated in a concrete task.

Comparing explicit Gaussian primitive motion against Eulerian grid-based fields (e.g., Pyro for smoke) or fluid particle dynamics lacks a formalized evaluation protocol or alignment formulation in the text.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in dynamic novel view synthesis (DyNVS) by moving beyond pure photorealism toward physical realism and multi-body interactions.

Comprehensive material coverage encompassing four distinct regimes (liquids, gases, rheological materials, and textiles) generated via industry-standard physics solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, XPBD) in Houdini.

Provides complete physical ground truth, including 3D particle trajectories and material parameters (e.g., Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, viscosity, temperature fields), enabling rigorous quantitative evaluation of physical plausibility.
Introduces sensible evaluation metrics for physical motion plausibility (Trajectory Distance and Area Under the Outlier Percentages) to assess primitive drift over time.

Thorough benchmarking of five recent dynamic 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting methods under both monocular and multi-view setups, clearly exposing failure modes of existing appearance-driven representations on complex dynamic phenomena.
weaknesses: The dataset scale is relatively modest, comprising only 17 scenes in total (roughly 4 scenes per material type), which limits statistical variety across scenarios.

Evaluation of physical realism metrics (TD and AUOP in Table 6) is only reported for two scenes ('Cow' and 'Box-smoke') rather than across the entire benchmark, leaving open questions about trajectory tracking performance in liquid and textile interaction scenes.

The trajectory matching approach for TD/AUOP pairs reconstructed primitives to ground-truth particles based on Euclidean nearest-neighbor distance at the initial frame; this heuristic can become unreliable or degenerate in fluid/smoke settings where topology changes, splitting, or significant density variations occur.
Video resolution is somewhat low (640x720) compared to contemporary NVS benchmarks, and the multi-view setting features only 2 to 4 moving camera views.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: bridging the gap between visual photorealism and physical plausibility in Dynamic Novel View Synthesis (DyNVS).

Provides diverse material behaviors across four distinct physical categories (liquids, gases, rheological materials, and textiles) using appropriate physical solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, XPBD) rather than a single simplified simulator.

Supplies complete ground-truth physical quantities, including 3D particle trajectories and physical parameters (e.g., Young's modulus, viscosity, temperature fields), which are virtually impossible to acquire accurately from real-world dynamic video.

Offers a thorough evaluation of existing DyNVS methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, MoSca, SoM) across both monocular and multi-view setups, clearly exposing failure modes such as needle-like artifacts and surface-only motion hallucinations.
Proposes two physical realism metrics (Trajectory Distance and Area Under the Outlier Percentages) to quantitatively assess motion fidelity of reconstructed primitives.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively modest, comprising only 17 synthetic scenes in total (approximately 4 scenes per material type), which limits the overall diversity of geometries and interaction configurations.

The trajectory evaluation metric relies on a nearest-neighbor matching heuristic in the initial frame ($t=0$). In 4D Gaussian Splatting, primitives frequently undergo adaptive density control (densification, splitting, and pruning), meaning primitives may not correspond consistently to physical mass particles across time, which could bias or distort the Trajectory Distance (TD) and AUOP calculations.

The visual appearance of many scenes remains somewhat artificial (e.g., basic checkerboard planes, simple primitive colliders, synthetic lighting), which creates a domain gap between these benchmark simulations and real-world dynamic video captures.
The exploration of inverse physics parameter estimation in Section 5.3 is very preliminary, evaluated on only a single scene ('bouncing balls') with two baseline methods.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: moving dynamic novel view synthesis (DyNVS) beyond pure appearance reconstruction toward physics-informed reasoning and multi-body interactions.

Comprehensive physical ground truth: by generating scenes via established Houdini solvers (FLIP, Pyro, MPM, XPBD), the dataset provides authentic 3D particle flow trajectories and constitutive parameters (viscosity, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, temperature).

Novel evaluation metrics for physical realism: the introduced Trajectory Distance (TD) and Area Under the Outlier Percentages (AUOP) provide a standardized way to evaluate whether dynamic primitives genuinely follow underlying physics rather than merely overfit visual appearance.

Thorough benchmarking and insightful analysis: evaluates multiple representative 4DGS methods (D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, MoSca, SoM) across both monocular and multiview settings, demonstrating their failure cases (e.g., surface fluttering, floaters, and needle-like artifacts under complex dynamics) as well as evaluating inverse physics estimation models.
weaknesses: Modest dataset scale: the benchmark contains only 17 scenes across four material classes (~4 scenes per material type), which limits statistical diversity.

Nearest-neighbor trajectory matching sensitivity: matching reconstructed Gaussian primitives to ground-truth trajectories based solely on Euclidean distance at frame 0 (Eq. 1) can be noisy or biased if primitive positions at t=0 are sparser, offset, or represent optical boundaries rather than material mass centers.

Absence of a physics-integrated DyNVS baseline in the dynamic rendering benchmark: while inverse parameter identification is tested in Section 5.3 with PAC-NeRF and GIC, the dynamic novel view synthesis benchmark (Table 4–6) only evaluates non-physics 4DGS baselines. Demonstrating how a physics-regularized baseline (e.g., Spring-Gaus or PhysGaussian) performs on TD/AUOP would make the benchmark even more compelling.
Relatively low video resolution (640x720) and limited multi-view coverage (2 to 4 camera trajectories).
